source.title: When Safety Becomes a Vulnerability: Exploiting LLM Alignment Homogeneity for Transferable Blocking in RAG
source.authors: Jun-Cheng Li; Chaoyang Qi; Rong-Zheng Wang; Qi-Zhi Chen; Liang Xu; Di Liang; B. Simons; Shuang Liang

record.file_problem: none; full paper text and appendices are present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper uses a refusal-direction analysis as a tool for comparing RAG blocking methods, but does not causally test the claimed direction by ablating or adding it. Its blocking attacks induce refusals through retrieved context rather than testing the claimed residual-stream intervention.
record.gate_note: Appendix B constructs a weighted refusal-minus-compliance direction and measures calibrated activation projections for several RAG attack contexts. It does not use the claim's harmful-minus-harmless difference-in-means recipe or intervene on the direction. The main attack-success results concern refusals deliberately induced by poisoned RAG context; they do not test whether the claimed direction mediates refusal. Layer selection and projection calibration are analysis procedures, not separate outcome rows.
record.test_reason: The paper is a RAG blocking-attack study. Its only use of a refusal direction is Appendix B, where a weighted refusal-minus-compliance direction (Cyberey et al.'s recipe) serves as a diagnostic for its own attack. It projects inputs onto this direction to compare TabooRAG with baseline attacks. It never ablates or adds the direction, never tests whether the direction mediates refusal, and induces refusal on purpose through crafted context. So it uses the finding as a tool to explain its method's performance (T4) and tests no version.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors conclude that safety-aligned LLMs share risk categories and refusal criteria ('alignment homogeneity'). This lets a single surrogate-optimized risk-context document induce refusals across unknown target models, with a mean ASR_PG of 62.1%. Appendix B's projections are offered as supporting representation-level evidence, not as a causal test of the direction.
record.recipe_differences: Uses a weighted mean difference between refusal and compliance activations, with a neutral-set reference and calibrated projection scores; it does not use the original harmful-minus-harmless direction procedure or perform ablation/addition.
record.method_sensitivity: The direction is constructed from last-token residual activations at a selected layer; each model is calibrated separately using 300 safe Alpaca and 100 harmful JailbreakBench reference projections. The selected layer and numerical projection values are not stated in the text.

fits_no_version.finding: On five open models, TabooRAG contexts project right-shifted (refusal-like) on a weighted refusal direction. MutedRAG, Jamming and WDoS shift toward the safe side on more capable models, but MutedRAG and WDoS still cross the boundary on Llama-3-8B. All results are figure-only.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Refusal-inducing RAG contexts move last-token activations toward a refusal direction, in proportion to their behavioural blocking success; this is observational only.

record.problems: The direction analysis is observational: no direction ablation or addition is performed. Projection outcomes are shown only as figures, without numerical values or uncertainty intervals. The paper reports uncertainty for other outcomes, including run-to-run standard deviations and statistical tests, but not for the plotted projection distributions.
record.rows_left_out: Main attack-success rates and robustness results are not included: they measure refusals deliberately induced by poisoned RAG context, not effects of the residual-stream direction. They are reported in Tables 1–8 and 13–24. The safe and harmful reference projection sets are used for calibration rather than reported as separate outcomes for a version of the claim.

untested.parts: No ablation or addition of the direction; no capability check.
The attacks induce refusal rather than suppress it; no adversarial training against ablation.
No multi-direction or cone analysis of activations. The eigenvalue analysis in Appendix D concerns cross-model outcome correlations, not residual-stream directions.
Each model gets its own direction; transfer of a direction is not tested. Only attack documents are transferred.

record.verdict_notes: Arditi et al. [1] is cited only as motivation for the claim that refusal is 'a low-dimensional direction'. The direction recipe follows Cyberey et al. and is calibrated per model on Alpaca and JailbreakBench. The layer and numerical values are not reported. The behavioural ASR tables concern deliberately induced refusal and were correctly left out as rows.

versions.untested_parts: No ablation or addition of a harmful-minus-harmless direction; no test of effects on refusal or general capabilities.
No weight edit or released-model abliteration.
The blocking attacks aim to induce refusals, not suppress refusal; no test of jailbreak suppression of the direction or robustness training against its ablation.
No comparison of affine, cone, or multiple residual-stream refusal directions. The paper’s shared statistical direction concerns cross-model blocking outcomes, not residual-stream directions.
No separation of harmfulness judgments from refusal decisions.
The paper transfers blocking documents across models, not a refusal direction across languages, model variants, or base-to-instruct models.
No manipulation or comparison of refusal training methods or timing.
No evaluation of reasoning models or models that reason before answering.
